Contingent risk assessment formalizes decision-making under uncertainty by assigning numerical probabilities to outcomes. When such probabilities are known, rational behavior becomes possible through expected utility maximization. This principle underpins both GSI's Bayesian inference and GSE's state-transition logic. Insurance exemplifies how aggregating many independent risks transforms variable costs into predictable fixed expenses—a core tenet of risk management. The mathematical duality lies in treating uncertainty as either stochastic variability (GSI) or deterministic policy response (GSE). Failure modes include overconfidence in probability estimates and misapplication of aggregation principles beyond their domain of validity.
